questionText: `public class Singleton { private static Singleton instance; private Singleton() {} public static Singleton getInstance(){ if(instance == null){ instance = new Singleton(); return instance; } return instance; } }`. What does making the constructor private, combined with getInstance(), actually achieve?
option1: It makes the class abstract, so it cannot be instantiated at all
option2: It allows unlimited instances to be created, but only through getInstance()
option3: It has no real effect, private constructors behave identically to public ones
option4: It makes it impossible for any code outside the Singleton class to call new Singleton() directly -- the only way to obtain a Singleton object from outside is through the public getInstance() method, which controls exactly how many instances ever get created
correctOptionExplanation: Private constructor plus a controlled access point (getInstance) is the entire mechanism behind Singleton.

questionText: `Singleton s1 = Singleton.getInstance(); Singleton s2 = Singleton.getInstance();`. What is s1 == s2?
option1: false, since getInstance() is called twice
option2: true -- the first call creates the object and stores it in the static instance field; the second call sees instance is no longer null and returns that exact same stored reference, so s1 and s2 point to the identical object in memory
option3: This causes a compile error since Singleton has no public constructor
option4: It depends on whether Singleton overrides equals()
correctOptionExplanation: Both calls return references to the same stored object once it has been created.

questionText: `Singleton s1 = Singleton.getInstance(); System.out.println(s1); Singleton s2 = Singleton.getInstance(); System.out.println(s2);`. Since Singleton does not override toString(), what do the two printed lines look like relative to each other?
option1: They print the exact same text, e.g. Singleton@1b6d3586 twice -- since s1 and s2 are the same object, the default Object.toString() output (class name plus hashcode) is identical both times
option2: They print two different hashcodes since two println calls happened
option3: They print "null" both times since instance starts as null
option4: This throws a NullPointerException on the second println
correctOptionExplanation: Same object means the default toString() output (class name plus hashcode) is identical both times.

questionText: If Main.java tried Singleton s = new Singleton(); directly instead of calling getInstance(), what happens?
option1: It compiles and creates a second, independent Singleton object
option2: It compiles, but silently returns the existing shared instance instead of creating a new one
option3: Compile error -- Singleton()'s constructor is private, so it is not accessible from Main (a different class), and Java refuses to compile the direct instantiation
option4: It compiles, but throws a runtime exception the first time it's called
correctOptionExplanation: A private constructor cannot be called from any class other than the one that declares it.

questionText: Inside Singleton.getInstance(), the line instance = new Singleton(); calls the same private constructor. Why does this compile, when Main.java calling new Singleton() does not?
option1: getInstance() is a special method name that Java exempts from access checks
option2: Static methods are always allowed to call any constructor, private or not
option3: This is actually a bug in the code and shouldn't compile
option4: private restricts access to code outside the class -- it does not restrict the class from calling its own private members from within itself; getInstance() is defined inside Singleton, so it's allowed to call Singleton's own private constructor, the same rule that let processOrder() call private helper methods inside PaymentProcessor
correctOptionExplanation: Privacy is a boundary around the class, not a restriction on the class calling its own members.

questionText: The class notes ask: can we keep the instance field final for the lazy Singleton above? What's the answer, and why?
option1: Yes, marking it final has no effect on lazy initialization either way
option2: No -- final static fields must be assigned at declaration or inside a static initializer block, never inside a regular method; since instance is intentionally assigned lazily inside getInstance() (only on the first call), the compiler will not allow final here
option3: Yes, but only if getInstance() is also marked final
option4: No, because static fields can never be marked final in Java under any circumstance
correctOptionExplanation: Lazy assignment inside a normal method is fundamentally incompatible with the final keyword's assignment rules.

questionText: `public class Singleton { private static final Singleton instance = new Singleton(); private Singleton() {} public static Singleton getInstance() { return instance; } }`. Is this valid, and what's the real trade-off compared to the lazy version?
option1: Valid -- the assignment happens right at declaration, which satisfies final's rules, so getInstance() no longer needs a null check at all; the trade-off is this object gets created the moment the class loads, whether or not getInstance() is ever called, whereas the lazy version only pays that cost on first use
option2: Invalid, new Singleton() cannot appear in a field initializer
option3: Valid, and behaves identically to the lazy version in every respect
option4: Valid, but getInstance() must still contain an if-null check for this to work correctly
correctOptionExplanation: Eager initialization trades upfront creation cost for a simpler getInstance() with no null check needed.

questionText: Class Reporter and class Logger both independently call Singleton.getInstance() somewhere in their own code. Do they end up holding different Singleton objects?
option1: Yes, each calling class gets its own separate instance
option2: Only if Reporter and Logger are in different packages
option3: No -- there is exactly one Singleton instance for the entire application, stored once in the static instance field; every caller anywhere receives a reference to that same single object
option4: It depends on the order in which Reporter and Logger are loaded
correctOptionExplanation: The static field is shared at the class level, so every caller everywhere gets the same object.

questionText: `public static Singleton getInstance(){ return new Singleton(); }` (bug: missing the null check entirely). What does this broken version do to the Singleton guarantee?
option1: Nothing changes, Java automatically prevents more than one instance from being constructed
option2: This causes a compile error since new Singleton() cannot appear inside getInstance()
option3: This throws a runtime exception on the second call
option4: It completely breaks the pattern -- every call to getInstance() now constructs and returns a brand-new object, so Singleton.getInstance() == Singleton.getInstance() would now be false; nothing in the language enforces only one instance, the whole guarantee lives entirely in this method's logic being written correctly
correctOptionExplanation: The Singleton guarantee is entirely a matter of correct logic in getInstance() -- Java does not enforce it structurally.

questionText: Suppose Singleton()'s constructor has no access modifier at all (package-private) instead of private. Does the singleton guarantee still hold?
option1: Yes, package-private is just as restrictive as private for this purpose
option2: No -- any other class within the same package could still call new Singleton() directly, bypassing getInstance() entirely and creating additional instances; only private fully closes off construction to everyone except the class itself
option3: Yes, because getInstance() would still be the only public way to reach it
option4: No, but only if the other class is in a different package
correctOptionExplanation: Package-private still permits any class in the same package to construct additional instances directly.

questionText: A developer proposes making Singleton an abstract class instead of giving it a private constructor, believing this also guarantees only one instance. Is this correct?
option1: No -- declaring a class abstract only prevents that specific class from being instantiated directly; it does not limit the total number of objects in existence, and does not relate to controlling instance count the way a private constructor plus getInstance() does. Abstract classes solve a different problem (deferring implementation to subclasses)
option2: Yes, abstract classes and Singletons are functionally identical
option3: Yes, since abstract classes can never be instantiated at all, by anyone, ever
option4: No, but only because abstract classes cannot have static methods
correctOptionExplanation: Abstract classes prevent direct instantiation of that class, but concrete subclasses could still be instantiated any number of times -- this is not the Singleton mechanism at all.

questionText: `public class PlayState implements IState { private static final PlayState singleton = new PlayState(); private PlayState(){} public static PlayState getInstance(){ return singleton; } ... }`. Which initialization style is this, and why is it reasonable specifically for a State Pattern implementation?
option1: Lazy initialization -- it defers creating PlayState until the first time play() is called on it
option2: This is neither eager nor lazy, it's a third, unrelated initialization style unique to interfaces
option3: Eager initialization -- the single PlayState object is created immediately when the class loads. This is reasonable here specifically because PlayState (like the other IState implementations) holds no per-instance data, so there is no real downside to creating it upfront, and it removes the need for a null check
option4: Lazy initialization, since the field could theoretically be reassigned later
correctOptionExplanation: Assignment at declaration is eager initialization, a natural fit for a stateless object with no construction cost concerns.

questionText: PlayState.getInstance() just does return singleton; with no null check. Why is that safe here, unlike the plain Singleton.java example?
option1: It isn't actually safe, and this is a bug in the code
option2: Java automatically adds a null check to every static getInstance() method
option3: PlayState doesn't need a null check because it implements an interface
option4: Because singleton is assigned eagerly, right at declaration, it is guaranteed to already be a valid, non-null object by the time the class finishes loading -- long before getInstance() could ever possibly be called, so there is nothing left to check
correctOptionExplanation: Eager initialization guarantees the field is populated before any code could possibly call getInstance().

questionText: `public class MediaPlayer { private IState state = StopState.getInstance(); ... }`. What does this line demonstrate about how MediaPlayer relates to the Singleton pattern?
option1: MediaPlayer creates its own private StopState object, separate from any other MediaPlayer
option2: MediaPlayer is a client of the StopState singleton -- it retrieves and stores a reference to the one shared StopState object that getInstance() always returns, rather than constructing a fresh StopState of its own; every MediaPlayer that starts out stopped ends up pointing at that exact same StopState instance
option3: This line will not compile since StopState's constructor is private
option4: MediaPlayer must itself implement IState for this line to work
correctOptionExplanation: MediaPlayer never constructs its own StopState -- it just asks the Singleton for the one that already exists.

questionText: `player.play(); player.stop(); System.out.println(player.getState());`. Since none of IState, PlayState, PauseState, StopState override toString(), what does this actually print?
option1: Something like StopState@1540e19d -- the default Object.toString() implementation: fully-qualified class name, @, and the object's hashcode in hex; no friendly readable label unless toString() is overridden
option2: The literal text "Stopped"
option3: A NullPointerException, since getState() returns an interface type
option4: The word "IState" followed by the method name last called
correctOptionExplanation: Without an overridden toString(), Java falls back to the default class-name-plus-hashcode format.

questionText: In Main.java, at two different points, the call sequence happens to leave player in StopState both times, and println(player.getState()) runs at both points. Do the two printed lines show the exact same hashcode?
option1: No, each transition into StopState creates a distinct object with its own hashcode
option2: Only if MediaPlayer itself is also a Singleton
option3: Yes -- StopState.getInstance() always returns the exact same shared object no matter how many times or from where it is called, so player.getState() at both points references that identical single StopState instance, and the printed hashcode is identical both times
option4: No, hashcodes are randomized on every println call in Java
correctOptionExplanation: Because StopState is a Singleton, every reference to it anywhere in the program is the same object with the same hashcode.

questionText: Why does it make sense to implement each IState (PlayState, PauseState, StopState) as its own Singleton, specifically in a State Pattern context?
option1: It does not make sense, State Pattern and Singleton should never be combined
option2: It is required by Java -- any class implementing an interface with no fields must be a Singleton
option3: It makes MediaPlayer itself thread-safe automatically
option4: Since these state objects are stateless, the exact same object can safely be reused everywhere it is needed; wrapping each one in a Singleton enforces that there is only ever one shared instance by construction, rather than relying on every developer remembering to reuse existing objects instead of writing new PlayState() out of habit
correctOptionExplanation: Singleton turns the 'stateless objects are safely shareable' optimization into a guaranteed rule, not just a convention.

questionText: Suppose StopState.play() instead did player.setState(new PlayState()), constructing a fresh PlayState on every transition, instead of calling PlayState.getInstance(). Would the State Pattern still function correctly?
option1: No, this would break the transitions entirely and the code would misbehave
option2: It would still function correctly -- every PlayState object ever created behaves identically, since none hold any data. The only real downside is wastefulness: a brand-new object gets created on every transition into that state, even though reusing the one existing instance would have worked just as well
option3: No, because PlayState's constructor is private and cannot be called with new from StopState
option4: Yes, and it would actually be faster than using the Singleton version
correctOptionExplanation: Correctness would be preserved since PlayState is stateless, but every fresh construction would be pure waste.

questionText: Why does PlayState also declare its own constructor private, the same way the standalone Singleton.java example does?
option1: For exactly the same reason as any Singleton -- to guarantee that nothing (not MediaPlayer, not another state class, not any future code) can accidentally construct a second PlayState with new PlayState(); every caller is forced through getInstance(), which always hands back the one existing shared object
option2: Because IState requires all of its implementing classes to have private constructors
option3: It is not actually necessary here and could safely be made public with no consequence
option4: To prevent PlayState from being assigned to a variable of type IState
correctOptionExplanation: The private constructor closes off every possible route to a second PlayState object, same reasoning as any Singleton.

questionText: MediaPlayer's field is private IState state = StopState.getInstance();, calling the Singleton directly inside the class. If you wanted to unit-test MediaPlayer with a fake IState instead of the real StopState, how easy is that, compared to how AreaCalculator/ShoppingCart received their dependencies earlier in the course?
option1: Just as easy -- Singleton and constructor injection provide identical testing flexibility
option2: Impossible under any circumstances to test MediaPlayer at all
option3: Noticeably harder -- MediaPlayer reaches out and grabs StopState.getInstance() itself, hardcoding a dependency directly inside its own field initializer, the same way a class calling new ConcreteClass() internally could not be tested with a fake. Earlier examples receiving dependencies through the constructor (like AreaCalculator receiving List<Shape2D>) could simply be handed a mock instead -- MediaPlayer as written here does not offer that seam
option4: Easier, because Singletons are automatically mockable in Java without any extra work
correctOptionExplanation: Reaching out to a Singleton directly is a hard-coded dependency, the same testing problem as internally constructing a concrete class.

questionText: A team decides every class in their application -- OrderService, UserProfile, ShoppingCart -- should be turned into a Singleton "just to be safe and consistent." Is this good practice?
option1: Yes, more Singletons always make an application more predictable
option2: Yes, since Singleton is the recommended default for every class unless proven otherwise
option3: It has no real downside either way
option4: No -- most of these classes genuinely need multiple independent instances (different carts for different users, different orders per purchase); forcing them into a single shared instance turns them into hidden global mutable state that many unrelated parts of the code can silently read and modify. Singleton fits classes that conceptually should only ever have one instance, not arbitrary business objects
correctOptionExplanation: Overusing Singleton for objects that genuinely need multiple instances creates hidden global state and hurts maintainability.

questionText: Java's reflection API lets code call constructor.setAccessible(true) on a private constructor and then invoke it directly. Does this mean even a correctly-written Singleton can technically end up with more than one instance?
option1: Yes -- reflection can bypass the normal private access check entirely and construct a second object directly, sidestepping getInstance() completely; a private constructor alone is not a 100% unbreakable guarantee against every possible way code could try to create an instance, only against normal, non-reflective instantiation
option2: No, private is absolute and cannot be bypassed by any Java code under any circumstances
option3: No, but only because getInstance() is also marked private
option4: Yes, but only if the Singleton class implements an interface
correctOptionExplanation: Reflection can bypass normal access modifiers, so a private constructor alone is not an absolute guarantee against a second instance.

questionText: `public class ConfigManager { private static ConfigManager instance; private String configPath; private ConfigManager(String configPath){ this.configPath = configPath; } public static ConfigManager getInstance(String configPath){ if(instance == null){ instance = new ConfigManager(configPath); } return instance; } }`. getInstance("prod.properties") is called first, then later getInstance("test.properties") is called somewhere else. What configPath does the second caller actually end up with?
option1: "test.properties", since that is the value passed on the second call
option2: "prod.properties" -- the first call already constructed the one instance using "prod.properties"; the second call sees instance is no longer null and just returns that already-built object, completely ignoring the "test.properties" argument
option3: A brand new ConfigManager is created with "test.properties" and replaces the old one
option4: This throws an exception since getInstance() cannot be called twice with different arguments
correctOptionExplanation: Once constructed, the lazy Singleton ignores all future arguments passed to getInstance() -- a classic real-world API-design gotcha.

questionText: Once Singleton.getInstance() has been called for the first time, does the resulting object typically get garbage collected later while the application is still running and the class is still loaded?
option1: Yes, it gets collected as soon as no local variable references it anymore
option2: Yes, after a fixed timeout period set by the JVM
option3: No -- the object is referenced by the static field instance, and static fields hold a live reference for as long as their class remains loaded; since the class stays loaded for essentially the entire life of a typical running application, the single instance effectively lives for the whole application's lifetime
option4: It depends on whether getInstance() was called from main() or from another method
correctOptionExplanation: A static field keeps the referenced object alive for as long as the class stays loaded, which is normally the whole application run.

questionText: What's the actual difference in purpose between a Singleton class and a plain class made entirely of static methods with no instance at all?
option1: There is no meaningful difference, they solve the exact same problem
option2: A static utility class always uses more memory than an equivalent Singleton
option3: Singleton classes cannot have any methods, only static utility classes can
option4: A static utility class has no real object and no instance state at all, ever -- it is just a namespace for functions. A Singleton is a genuine single object with real instance behavior, and critically, that object can be passed around, stored in variables, and assigned to interface-typed references (like IState) -- something a bag of static methods fundamentally cannot do
correctOptionExplanation: A Singleton is a real object that can be passed around and assigned to interface types, unlike a namespace of static methods.

questionText: Could PlayState's behavior instead have been written as a class of pure static methods (no getInstance(), no implementing IState) and still worked correctly inside MediaPlayer's state field?
option1: Yes, static methods and Singleton objects are always interchangeable
option2: No -- MediaPlayer.state is declared as type IState, and only a real object implementing that interface can be assigned to it and be called polymorphically through state.play(this); a class of static methods has no object to assign to that field and cannot implement an interface the way a genuine Singleton instance can
option3: Yes, but only if MediaPlayer's field were changed from IState to String
option4: No, because interfaces in Java cannot have implementing classes at all
correctOptionExplanation: The IState-typed field requires an actual object implementing the interface -- static methods cannot fulfill that role.

questionText: The class notes show A a1 = A.getInstance(); printing 123, then A a2 = A.getInstance(); printing 123 again. What does this confirm, and which comparison correctly verifies it in code?
option1: It confirms a1 and a2 reference the exact same object; the correct way to verify this is a1 == a2, comparing object identity -- not a1.equals(a2), which by default just falls back to the same identity check anyway unless equals() has been overridden
option2: It confirms a1 and a2 have equal field values but are different objects, verified using .equals()
option3: It confirms getInstance() returns a String literal "123"
option4: It confirms A has exactly 123 instances in memory
correctOptionExplanation: The == operator is the direct, correct way to confirm two references point to the identical object.

questionText: In one sharp sentence -- why are PlayState, PauseState, and StopState implemented as Singletons rather than plain classes instantiated fresh on every transition?
option1: Because IState requires it as part of the Java interface contract
option2: Because MediaPlayer would fail to compile otherwise
option3: Because these state objects are stateless and behave identically no matter how many times they are constructed, so making each one a Singleton guarantees -- by construction, not by convention -- that only one instance of each ever exists and gets reused everywhere, eliminating both unnecessary object creation and the risk of a developer forgetting to reuse an existing instance
option4: Because Singleton is a mandatory requirement of every State Pattern implementation in every codebase
correctOptionExplanation: This ties Singleton and State together: stateless implementations are the ideal candidates for the Singleton guarantee.
